finding.headline: At age 67, delaying Social Security can raise your benefit until age 70.
details: Social Security benefits rise for each month you delay past full retirement age; the increase stops at age 70.
If you delay retirement, sign up for Medicare at age 65. Missing that sign-up can delay coverage and cost more.

finding.headline: You can count on $28,600 a year: $16,500 for basics and $12,100 for the rest.
details: Your basics cost about $16,500 a year.
Your spending goal of $26,000 a year lasts in 100 of 100 scenarios.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
You already get Social Security (from 67): the plan uses the $30,600 a year you gave.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 94. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.

needs.line: Your basics cost about $16,500 a year. They are paid in all 100 scenarios.

plan.headline: You can count on $28,600 a year: $16,500 for basics and $12,100 for the rest. That is less than your Social Security of $30,600 a year. That is because health costs come on top of your spending and tax takes part of it.
